name: Kira Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. We sell nothing, and your answers stay confidential. What happens on a usual workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Kira Olsen, 58, and I operate a dragline at a large mine. I inspect the ropes and bucket teeth before moving earth, then watch the swing so nobody enters the machine’s reach. I like making a clean cut, but I never get used to the noise of a tooth striking hidden rock.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is your household like now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Jon repairs boats part time, and our daughter and son are grown and living elsewhere. I have a vocational certificate and about three months of bills saved, so my mine pay matters. I use an AI assistant every day for manual searches and weather notes, even though I check the machine with my own eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that a quick manual search is worth having, even if the big promises go nowhere. I already use an AI assistant daily to find torque settings. It does not get to say whether a rope looks frayed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d welcome steady wages and a chance to top up our three-month savings. Jon’s boat repairs are patchy in winter, and I do not want to ask our grown children to cover a bill. A small tool is useful without being a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep operating the dragline and inspecting its ropes at the start of each shift. I’d save seventy from each pay packet during the first year, if Jon’s repair work covers its usual share. I’d continue checking each AI manual answer against the manufacturer’s page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm at work, maybe a little vindicated that the machine still needs an operator. The household cushion is the worry I already had. I would enjoy the tool’s small conveniences without making a ceremony of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the danger in a wrong torque setting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loose fastener can work its way out under vibration. I caught one wrong number in a summary last month, looked up the manufacturer’s page and called the fitter before moving the dragline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why seventy per pay packet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would add up without squeezing the grocery account when boat work is slow. Jon and I would check it after the first month and lower it if the bills demand.

say: I’d welcome a **quick manual search** while still checking the dragline ropes myself.
An AI assistant cannot judge a **frayed rope** from my cab.
think: I want **steady wages** to build more than three months of savings.
Jon’s winter **boat repairs** bring uneven income.
do: Operate the **dragline** and inspect ropes each shift.
Save **seventy** per pay packet if boat income covers its share.
Check AI torque answers against the **manufacturer manual**.
feel: **Calm** about work, with the existing savings gap still on my mind.
S0.quote: A small tool is useful without being a retirement plan.
fieldNote: Kira is a regular **AI user**, yet a previous wrong torque summary taught her to verify against the manufacturer.
She sets a **conditional savings amount** because Jon’s boat repairs can slow in winter.

steps.text: Keep operating the dragline after checking its ropes each shift
Save seventy per pay packet if boat income covers its share
Use the AI assistant for manual searches and verify torque settings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say buying and scheduling will change before anybody builds a robot that can run our dragline. I’d ask to test the new planning screen with the ground crew, because the swing radius is real even when a map looks tidy. Young apprentices should learn both the screen and the exclusion line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be useful in a trial, but I might also be asked to cover work that used to belong to the planners. I expect the operator roster to hold for now. I worry more immediately that cheaper automated repair booking could reduce the calls Jon gets for boats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the planner next week for access to the trial screen and mark any route that crosses the dragline’s exclusion line. I’d show the apprentice how to compare that map with the stakes on the ground. In the first year I’d keep my operating shifts and ask Jon each month what repair bookings actually came in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel curious at the mine and uneasy at home. I can learn a screen quickly, but that does not keep a customer calling Jon. I would rather measure his bookings than argue about a forecast over dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you seen a bad route on a screen before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The last digital map put a delivery truck beside our counterweight path. We moved its stop point after walking the ground, and I would bring that example to the software trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Jon change his business now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He would keep taking repair work and record calls for a few months first. A new booking app is not proof that my husband Jon’s customers have left.

say: I’d say **planning software** arrives before dragline robots.
I’d put ground crews in the trial to protect the **exclusion line**.
think: My operator roster likely holds, though I may absorb **planning checks**.
Jon’s **repair bookings** could shrink if customer booking changes.
do: Test the **planning screen** against the dragline exclusion line.
Show the **apprentice** how to check maps against ground stakes.
Keep operating shifts and count Jon’s **monthly bookings**.
feel: **Curious** at work and uneasy about household repair income.
S1.quote: A new booking app is not proof that my husband Jon’s customers have left.
fieldNote: Kira volunteers for the **planning trial** because she has already corrected a dangerous delivery stop near the counterweight.
Her greater worry is **Jon’s repair income**, which could shrink even while her own operating roster holds.

steps.text: Test AI planning routes against the dragline exclusion line
Keep operating the dragline and teach the apprentice ground checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell coworkers that full thinking AI in 2028 could remake planning before robots run the dragline around 2031. I would ask the mine for its equipment dates, not a lecture about innovation. Three years before dragline robots arrive is a short apprenticeship for a different life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 60 at the AI date and 63 when robots can operate as well as I can. I had counted on more mine wages before retirement, and three months of bills would go fast if those wages stop. Jon’s boat repairs cannot replace a mine wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the mine this month about advertised machine-maintenance posts and whether the certificate is funded. I’d enroll in the maintenance course and apply for the vacancy if the mine pays for training and posts a genuine opening. In 2029 I’d keep running the dragline while shifts exist and pause the plan to replace our kitchen floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel anxious, but I would have tasks for tomorrow morning. I cannot assume maintenance is safe forever when thinking AI and capable robots exist. I would tell Jon we need dates and prices before we decide whether I can stop working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a maintenance course worth it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want the fee paid and a posted job with actual shifts, not a badge to hang on the wall. A robot fleet could need repairs, but it might need fewer people too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children for help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter and son have their own rents and families. I would tell them what is happening, but I would look for paid work and cut the floor project first.

say: I’d ask for **equipment dates** rather than speeches.
I’d tell coworkers **2028 planning AI** comes before dragline robots around 2031.
think: At **63**, I might lose wages I expected before retirement.
Our **three-month cushion** and Jon’s repairs cannot replace mine pay.
do: Ask about funded **maintenance training** tied to a posted vacancy.
Keep dragline shifts in **2029** while they exist.
Pause the **kitchen floor** replacement to protect cash.
feel: **Anxious** about an early wage loss, while still able to seek funded work.
S2.quote: Three years before dragline robots arrive is a short apprenticeship for a different life.
fieldNote: Kira’s fast response is a **conditional maintenance course**, tied to funding and a real job opening.
She continues paid **dragline shifts** after 2028 but sees robots around 2031 as a threat to that income.

steps.text: Enroll in funded maintenance training if a genuine vacancy is posted
Apply for the posted mine maintenance vacancy if eligible
Keep running the dragline in 2029 while shifts exist
Pause the planned kitchen floor replacement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years is enough to teach an apprentice properly if the mine actually hires one. Full thinking AI arrives in 2031 and dragline robots around 2034, when I would be 66. I would want written terms for the older operators instead of a last-minute farewell meal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might be ready to retire at 66, but I have never checked what the retirement income would be beside our bills. Jon may still get boat work or may need to slow down. I cannot turn either guess into money on the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d get a retirement projection and write down our monthly costs with Jon now. I’d keep the dragline job and ask whether the mine offers a paid apprentice mentor post. In 2032 I’d compare any exit offer with our income plan before I agree to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy, though there is time to put numbers under the decision. I could enjoy teaching someone if I am paid to do it. I do not want a job title that disappears when robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach that an apprentice might miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put them beside the counterweight path and make them point out the safe line. A neat screen is no use if someone stands inside that swing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the retirement projection is low?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jon and I would keep my paid shifts while available and postpone replacing the car. I would ask our family for help only if we were truly short, after doing our own sums.

say: I’d ask for **written exit terms** before older operators leave.
I’d use the warning to teach an **apprentice** if the mine hires one.
think: At **66** when dragline robots arrive, retirement may fit, but we have not tested our income against bills.
do: Get a **retirement projection** and list monthly costs with Jon.
Keep paid dragline shifts and ask about a **mentor post**.
Compare any **2032 exit offer** with our household income plan.
feel: **Uneasy** but able to make a decision from figures.
S3.quote: I do not want a job title that disappears when robots arrive.
fieldNote: The later **2034 robot date** approaches Kira’s possible retirement, but she has not proved the household can afford it.
She would mentor an **apprentice for pay** if a post exists, rather than treat a title as secure work.

steps.text: Keep paid dragline shifts through 2032 if available
Wait for a retirement projection and exit offer before leaving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew a decade lets us write down the dangerous corners of the pit before old operators go. Thinking AI in 2036 will change office work first, and dragline robots around 2039 arrive when I’d be 71. I would rather watch my grandchildren than a dragline control screen at 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be 68 when the thinking AI arrives, and I hope to have stopped full shifts by then. I cannot promise it until Jon and I know whether savings and retirement income cover our bills. Ten years gives us a chance to build that cushion and avoid putting a burden on our children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d review our savings and expected retirement income every year with Jon. I’d keep paid dragline shifts while my health allows and bank half of any extra shift pay. In 2037 I’d retire if our income covers essentials; if it does not, I’d seek shorter paid shifts at the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel fairly calm about robots reaching my machine after my likely working years. I’d still be alert to our account balance and Jon’s health. That is the kind of uncertainty a family can work through with enough time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be in the pit notes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d mark the old soft patch near the west cut and the safe counterweight line. I’d hand those notes to the next operator and walk the places with them if the mine gives us a shift together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you invest in a robot for Jon’s repair work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, his part-time boat work is too small to justify a costly machine. We would build savings from mine pay and keep repair tools that already earn their keep.

say: I’d use the **decade** to record dangerous pit spots.
I hope to leave the **dragline** before robots arrive around 2039.
think: At **68** in 2036, retirement depends on savings and actual income.
I want to avoid putting a **burden** on our grown children.
do: Review **retirement income** with Jon every year.
Keep paid shifts and bank half of **extra-shift pay**.
Check **2037 essentials** before retiring or asking for shorter paid shifts.
feel: **Calm** about the late robot date, with family finances still in view.
S4.quote: I would rather watch my grandchildren than a dragline control screen at 71.
fieldNote: Kira sees the **2039 robot date** as likely beyond her dragline career, but her finances and Jon’s health still matter.
She would leave **pit safety notes** and walk the danger spots with a successor if given a shared shift.

steps.text: Keep paid dragline shifts while health and the roster allow
Bank half of any extra-shift pay after checking household bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because dragline robots around 2031 could stop my pay at 63. I need real equipment dates, funded training tied to a vacancy and clear retirement figures. I can take a risk on a course if the job behind it is real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the apprentice when every experienced operator is busy preparing to leave. Somebody needs paid time to walk the exclusion line with them. I can search a manual in seconds, but I cannot teach a safe distance from a kitchen chair.

headlineQuote: I can search a manual in seconds, but I cannot teach a safe distance from a kitchen chair.
portrait: Kira, **58**, runs a dragline and inspects ropes before moving earth at a large mine.
She uses **AI daily**, verifies manuals and volunteers to test new planning screens.
Mine pay supports a **three-month cushion** while Jon’s boat repairs vary.
Fast robots threaten her remaining wages; she considers **funded maintenance training** only with a genuine vacancy.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries Kira most because dragline robots around 2031 could stop her wages at 63.
whatWouldHelp: Real **equipment dates**, funded training tied to a vacancy and clear retirement figures would help her decide.
